Question: As a computer engineer what coding languages should I learn (name them please)?

I know it’s more than 40, though the vast majority of my work has been in only six of those. So the trick is to learn how to learn languages quickly. You do this by learning lots of languages early on. But first, you have to learn programming, which is a language-independent skill. Unfortunately, you have to learn a whole stack of things simultaneously when you start out: programming itself, debugging, some language, and some set of tools that will let you use that language (an editor, maybe a build system, maybe a debugger, version control…) Your first language should probably be something relatively easy, as you have all that extra load to deal with. Easy languages, however, are not typically the really important languages, either important because they’re widely used in industry, or important because of what they teach you. Question: Can a transport layer protocol be created that has better performance than TCP and UDP?
Old_Answer: Sure. You do have to define ‘performance’ and ‘better’, though, because there are multiple possible definitions and the differences matter. QUIC (as used in HTTP/3) may be the leading contender for that better protocol. But SCTP, DTLS, LEDBAT, and a few others, might also be better, depending on what exactly you want. If you are working in this field, you also need to be aware that QUIC, TCP, and SCTP are all moving targets; they get frequent upgrades too. So what it means to be “better than TCP” may not remain the same from month to month.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Yes, it’s certainly possible to create a transport layer protocol that outperforms TCP and UDP in certain scenarios. Both TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) have their strengths and weaknesses. TCP is reliable and ensures data integrity through its connection-oriented nature, but this comes at the cost of increased latency due to its handshaking process and congestion control mechanisms. On the other hand, UDP is faster and more efficient for applications that can tolerate some data loss, like streaming or gaming, but it lacks reliability and ordering guarantees. A new protocol could combine the best of both worlds by implementing a more efficient congestion control algorithm that adapts dynamically to network conditions, allowing for lower latency while still providing reliability. For instance, protocols like QUIC, developed by Google, already demonstrate this potential by offering multiplexing, reduced latency, and built-in encryption. Additionally, a new protocol could leverage techniques such as forward error correction to enhance reliability without the overhead of retransmissions. However, creating a universally better protocol is challenging due to the diverse nature of applications and network environments. What works well for one use case may not be suitable for another. Ultimately, the success of a new transport layer protocol will depend on its ability to address specific needs while maintaining compatibility with existing systems and infrastructure.

On the other hand, while UDP offers lower latency due to its connectionless nature, it sacrifices reliability and ordered delivery. Question: Do multiple people sharing an Internet connection each have their own unique external IP address?
Old_Answer: Most of the time, in IPv4, no. Almost always in IPv6, yes.
